newsitem.title: JAPAN: More Japan construction firms seen going under.
newsitem.headline: More Japan construction firms seen going under.

text.p: Japan's beleaguered construction sector has been hit by two high-profile failures this month, and the continued economic slump will likely bring more bankruptcies, analysts say.

Medium-sized general contractor Tada Corp applied for court protection from creditors under Japan's bankruptcy laws on Wednesday, weeks after similar move by Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd, which became the first publicly traded construction firm to go bust since World War II.
Wednesday's news reinforced market jitters over the fragile health of the construction industry, still burdened with massive "bubble era" debt.

Led by Tokai Kogyo, construction firms including JDC Corp, Daisue Construction Co Ltd, Daito Kogyo Co Ltd, Fujiko Co Ltd, Shokusan Jutaku Sogo Co Ltd and Aoki Corp dominated the top percentage losers list on the Tokyo bourse's first section on Thursday.
The slippage came when the market's benchmark Nikkei 225 average ended the day modestly higher.
Most of the issues have fallen below 300 yen ($2.54) or in some cases 100 yen (85 cents), a signal of no-confidence by the investment community.
"A stock price of below 200 yen ($1.70) means that the shares are labelled as disqualified for investment," said Etsusuke Masuda, an analyst at HSBC James Capel in Tokyo.

Japan's construction sector now has some 10 trillion yen ($84.7 billion) worth of interest-bearing debt, and a likely rise in domestic interest rates would make it hard for some firms in the sector to pay interest to banks, analysts said.
Japanese banks, which are just emerging from mountains of bad loans no longer have the will or the ability to stop construction firms from going under.
"I think more general contractors will be weeded out in the face of tough competition," said Rokuro Morimoto, a senior research at Tokyo Shoko Research, a credit research firm.
"It's hard to predict (how many construction firms will go under), but in the current financial year, I would be glad if the number was kept at around three to four," he said.
Once financial worries hit a construction company there is limited scope a recovery, since the doubts hit the order book and makes subcontractors wary of doing business with the company.
Worsening the outlook, Japan's government is tightening its budgetary belt by cutting down public spending.
The latest figures released by the Construction Ministry on Thursday showed no signs of a recovery in the construction sector.

Orders received by 50 major Japanese construction firms in June fell 6.5 percent from a year earlier to 1.30 trillion yen ($11.0 billion). Japan's housing starts meanwhile slipped 11.6 percent in June from a year ago, falling for the sixth consecutive month on a year-on-year basis, the ministry said.

"There had been a myth that listed general contractors would not go bankrupt, which had helped delay the write-offs of bad assets. It would actually be positive for the industry as a whole if this myth is proved wrong," said Masuda. ($1=118 yen)
